title: A music box’s steel comb was invented to save space: it replaced a stack of bells

cover.alt: Close-up inside an antique music box: a brass cylinder studded with tiny pins lies beside a polished steel comb with dozens of fine teeth.
cover.credit: Kijk- en Luistermuseum (Collectie Gelderland) · CC BY-SA 4.0

body: Inside a music box, pins on a turning cylinder pluck the tuned teeth of a steel **comb**, each tooth sounding its own note. Earlier musical clocks rang little bells from a pinned barrel instead. In 1796 the Geneva clockmaker **Antoine Favre-Salomon** replaced the stack of bells with one comb of pre-tuned metal teeth to save space, and with the pinned barrel lying flat beside it the mechanism could play more varied and complex music.

slides.alt: Close-ups of an antique cylinder music box: a brass cylinder dotted with tiny pins turns slowly beside a long steel comb, seen from the side and then from above inside its wooden case.
slides.caption: A cylinder music box made by Nicole Frères in 1864, now in a Dutch museum. As the brass cylinder slowly turns, its pins pluck the teeth of the steel comb beside it.
slides.credit: Kijk- en Luistermuseum (Collectie Gelderland) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · excerpt
